passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to set a riddle before Israel. ‘A great eagle with great wings and long pinions, full of feathers of many colors, came to Lebanon and took away the top of the cedar’ (verse 3). It carried the top shoot to a land of merchants, and planted a seed of the land, which grew into a low, spreading vine turning toward the eagle (verses 4-6).

Then a second great eagle appeared, and the vine stretched its roots and branches toward it, hoping to be watered (verse 7). Will it flourish? Will its roots not be pulled up and its fruit stripped, so that it withers when the east wind strikes it (verses 9-10)?
passages.hearers:
The eagle, or possibly the griffon vulture, since the Hebrew word covers both, was a symbol of power and speed. The cedar of Lebanon was the grandest tree in the region, used in royal palaces and in Solomon's temple, so its top fits the royal house of David. A low, spreading vine pictures a humbled kingdom that could still live.

The east wind was the hot, dry desert wind that could wither crops in a day. A riddle like this made the hearers work out the meaning, and the meaning was close to home.
passages.later: Babylon took King Jehoiachin and his officials into exile (2 Kings 24:12). Then ‘the king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, king in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah’ (2 Kings 24:17).
passages.asks: The vine could have lived quietly but reached toward a stronger power. Ask where you look for security in the wrong place. And ask what keeping faith would look like where you are planted.

passages.t: A broken oath, and a tender sprig
passages.happening:
God explains the riddle. The king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and took its king and officials to Babylon. He made a covenant with one of the royal family and put him under oath, so that the kingdom would be humbled but survive (verses 12-14). ‘But this king rebelled against Babylon by sending his envoys to Egypt to ask for horses and a large army’ (verse 15). He will die in Babylon, and Pharaoh's army will not help him (verses 16-17). ‘As surely as I live, I will bring down upon his head My oath that he despised and My covenant that he broke’ (verse 19).

Then God makes his own promise. ‘I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar’ and plant a tender sprig on a high mountain of Israel (verse 22). It will become ‘a majestic cedar’, and birds of every kind will nest under it (verse 23). ‘I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The first eagle is Nebuchadnezzar. The top of the cedar is King Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC. The seed of the land is Zedekiah, Jehoiachin's uncle, whom Nebuchadnezzar made king and bound by oath. The second eagle is Pharaoh, to whom Zedekiah turned for horses and troops.

Treaties were solemn oaths sworn in the names of the gods, and breaking one was treated as a crime against them. Zedekiah had sworn by the LORD. That is why God calls the broken oath his own.

The last verses turn from judgment to hope. God himself will plant a new shoot from David's line, and it will shelter every kind of bird.
passages.later: Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, ‘who had made him swear by God’ (2 Chronicles 36:13). Isaiah promised, ‘a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse’ (Isaiah 11:1).
passages.hard:
Why does God hold Zedekiah to an oath sworn to a pagan conqueror who had invaded Judah?

It can seem strange for God to side with Babylon's claims over his own people. Ezekiel's reasoning is twofold. The oath was sworn in the LORD's name, and Israel's law treated such oaths as sacred; to swear by God and then break the oath was to treat his name as worthless. And the prophets of this period, Jeremiah as well as Ezekiel, taught that submission to Babylon was God's judgment on Judah, so rebellion against it was rebellion against God's discipline.

Some readers worry that this makes God an ally of empire. The chapter answers that worry in its final verses, where God, not Babylon, plants the true king, and the great trees of the earth learn that he brings the tall low and makes the low tall.
passages.asks: God makes the low tree tall and brings the tall tree down. Ask where you are trusting in what looks tall and strong. And ask what it means that God's hope often begins as a tender sprig.
